content.text: Reflection of Light
Introduction

Reflection is one of the most familiar and easily observed wave phenomena. Every time you look in a mirror, see your image in a still pond, or notice the glare of sunlight off a building window, you are observing the reflection of light. Reflection is not limited to light alone; all types of waves, including sound, water waves, and radio waves, can be reflected. However, the reflection of light is particularly important because it is the basis of how we see most objects and how many optical devices function.

In this lesson, we will explore the laws governing reflection, understand how images are formed in plane mirrors, distinguish between regular and diffuse reflection, and learn to draw accurate ray diagrams. These concepts form the foundation for understanding more advanced optical systems.
Key Concepts
What Is Reflection?

Reflection occurs when a wave encounters a boundary between two different media and bounces back into the original medium. When a ray of light hits a smooth surface such as a mirror, it bounces off the surface in a predictable way governed by a simple law.
To describe reflection precisely, we need to define several terms:
Incident ray:
The incoming ray of light that strikes the reflecting surface.
Reflected ray:
The ray of light that bounces off the reflecting surface.
Normal:
An imaginary line drawn perpendicular (at 90 degrees) to the reflecting surface at the point where the incident ray strikes. The normal is a reference line used to measure angles.
Angle of incidence ($\theta_i$):
The angle between the incident ray and the normal.
Angle of reflection ($\theta_r$):
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
Point of incidence:
The point on the reflecting surface where the incident ray strikes.
It is critically important to note that all angles in optics are measured from the normal, not from the surface. This is a convention used throughout physics.
The Law of Reflection
The behaviour of reflected light is governed by two simple rules known collectively as the law of reflection:
The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection:
\theta_i = \theta_r
The incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal all lie in the same plane.
These laws apply to all types of reflection, whether from mirrors, polished metals, water surfaces, or any other reflective boundary. They apply equally to all types of waves, not just light.
The law of reflection is remarkably straightforward, yet it accounts for an enormous range of optical phenomena, from the simple plane mirror to the complex reflecting telescopes used in astronomy.

Regular Reflection vs Diffuse Reflection
Regular (specular) reflection

occurs when light reflects off a smooth, flat surface such as a plane mirror, still water, or polished metal. Because the surface is smooth, the normals at every point on the surface are parallel. This means that a set of parallel incoming rays will produce a set of parallel reflected rays. Regular reflection produces clear, sharp images.
Diffuse reflection

occurs when light reflects off a rough or uneven surface, such as paper, a brick wall, or a rough road. Although the law of reflection is still obeyed at each tiny point on the surface, the surface irregularities mean that the normals at different points point in different directions. As a result, parallel incoming rays are reflected in many different directions, scattering the light. Diffuse reflection does not produce clear images, but it is actually more useful in everyday life because it allows us to see objects from many different angles. If all surfaces produced only regular reflection, we would only be able to see objects when positioned at exactly the right angle.

Most objects are visible because of diffuse reflection. When light from a lamp or the Sun hits an object like a book, the rough surface of the book scatters the light in all directions, allowing anyone in the room to see the book regardless of their position.
Plane Mirrors

A plane mirror is a flat, smooth reflecting surface, typically made of glass with a thin coating of silver or aluminium on the back. Plane mirrors are the most common type of mirror used in everyday life.

When you stand in front of a plane mirror, light rays from every point on your body travel to the mirror, reflect according to the law of reflection, and enter your eyes. Your brain interprets these reflected rays as if they had come from behind the mirror in straight lines. This creates the appearance of an image behind the mirror.
Image Properties in a Plane Mirror
The image formed by a plane mirror has several distinctive properties:
The image is virtual.

A virtual image is one that cannot be projected onto a screen. The light rays do not actually pass through the image location; they only appear to come from behind the mirror. If you placed a screen behind the mirror at the image location, no image would appear on it.
The image is the same size as the object.
There is no magnification or reduction. The image of your hand in a plane mirror is exactly the same size as your actual hand.
The image is the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.
If you stand 2 metres in front of a plane mirror, your image appears to be 2 metres behind the mirror. The total apparent distance between you and your image is 4 metres.
The image is upright (erect).
The image is not flipped upside down. If you raise your right hand, the image also has a raised hand at the top.
The image is laterally inverted.

Left and right are swapped. If you raise your right hand, the image appears to raise its left hand. This is why text appears reversed in a mirror. Lateral inversion occurs because the mirror reverses the direction perpendicular to its surface (front-to-back), which our brain interprets as a left-right swap.
Ray Diagrams for Plane Mirrors
Ray diagrams are a powerful tool for understanding how images are formed. To draw a ray diagram for a plane mirror:
Draw the mirror as a straight line with short hatching marks on the back side to indicate the reflecting surface.
Mark the position of the object (typically represented as an arrow) in front of the mirror.
Draw at least two rays from the top of the object to the mirror.
At each point where a ray hits the mirror, draw the normal (perpendicular to the mirror surface).
Apply the law of reflection: draw the reflected ray such that the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.
Extend the reflected rays behind the mirror using dashed lines. These dashed lines represent the apparent path of light as perceived by the observer.
The point where the extended dashed lines meet behind the mirror is the position of the image of the top of the object.
The image should be drawn as a dashed arrow to indicate that it is virtual.
Repeat for the base of the object if needed.

How We See Objects
It is important to understand the distinction between luminous and non-luminous objects:
Luminous objects
produce their own light (e.g., the Sun, a light bulb, a candle flame).
Non-luminous objects
do not produce their own light. We see them because they reflect light from luminous sources into our eyes.

When we look at an object in a mirror, the process involves light travelling from a source to the object, reflecting off the object to the mirror, reflecting off the mirror, and finally entering our eyes. Our brain traces the reflected rays back in straight lines, perceiving the image as being behind the mirror.
Mathematical Relationships
The Law of Reflection
The mathematical statement of the law of reflection is simply:
\theta_i = \theta_r
where
\theta_i
is the angle of incidence (measured from the normal) and
\theta_r
is the angle of reflection (measured from the normal).
Image Distance
For a plane mirror, if the object distance (from the object to the mirror) is
d_o
, then the image distance (from the mirror to the image) is
d_i
, and:
d_o = d_i
The image is always the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.

Rotation of the Reflected Ray
If a plane mirror is rotated by an angle
\alpha
while the incident ray remains fixed, the reflected ray rotates by
2\alpha
. This principle is used in instruments such as the galvanometer and the sextant.

Multiple Mirrors
When two plane mirrors are placed at an angle
\theta
to each other, the number of images
n
formed is given by:
n = \frac{360}{\theta} - 1
This formula works when
360/\theta
is a whole number. If the mirrors are placed at 90 degrees, the number of images is
. If they are parallel (
\theta = 0
), theoretically an infinite number of images is formed.
Worked Examples
Example 1: Applying the Law of Reflection
Problem:
A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of 35 degrees to the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection?
Solution:
First, recognise that the angle given (35 degrees) is measured from the surface, not from the normal. The angle of incidence is measured from the normal:
By the law of reflection:
\theta_r = \theta_i = 55°
The angle of reflection is 55 degrees (measured from the normal).

Example 3: Multiple Mirrors
Problem:
Two plane mirrors are placed at 60 degrees to each other. An object is placed between them. How many images are formed?
Solution:
Five images are formed.
Example 4: Mirror Rotation
Problem:
A plane mirror is rotated by 15 degrees. By how much does the reflected ray rotate?
Solution:
The reflected ray rotates by twice the angle of mirror rotation:
\text{Rotation of reflected ray} = 2 \times 15° = 30°
Example 5: Minimum Mirror Height
Problem:
A person who is 1.8 m tall wants to see their full body in a plane mirror. What is the minimum height of the mirror required, and how should it be positioned?
Solution:
To see a full-length image, the mirror needs to be only half the height of the person:
\text{Minimum mirror height} = \frac{1.8}{2} = 0.9 \text{ m}

The bottom edge of the mirror should be placed at half the distance from the floor to the person's eyes. This works because of the geometry of reflection: the light from the person's feet reflects off the bottom of the mirror into their eyes, and the path geometry shows that only half the height is needed. This result is independent of how far the person stands from the mirror.
Common Misconceptions
Misconception 1: Angles are measured from the surface

A very common error is to measure the angle of incidence and angle of reflection from the mirror surface rather than from the normal. Always remember that in optics, angles are measured from the normal (the line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence). If a question gives you an angle measured from the surface, you must subtract it from 90 degrees to get the angle from the normal.
Misconception 2: You need a full-length mirror to see your whole body

Many people believe that you need a mirror as tall as yourself to see your full reflection. In fact, you only need a mirror that is half your height. This is a direct consequence of the law of reflection and the geometry of the reflected rays.
Misconception 3: The image is on the surface of the mirror
The image in a plane mirror appears to be located behind the mirror, at the same distance behind the surface as the object is in front. The image is not on the mirror surface itself.
Misconception 4: Plane mirrors reverse left and right

It is often said that mirrors reverse left and right, but this is not strictly accurate. A mirror reverses front and back (the direction perpendicular to its surface). When you face a mirror, your front becomes the back of the image and vice versa. Our brains interpret this front-back reversal as a left-right reversal because we imagine the image as another person who has turned around to face us.
Misconception 5: Diffuse reflection does not obey the law of reflection

Some students think that because diffuse reflection scatters light in many directions, the law of reflection is not being obeyed. This is incorrect. The law of reflection is obeyed at every single point on the rough surface. The scattering occurs because the normals at different points on the rough surface point in different directions, causing each reflected ray to head in a different direction.
Practice Problems
Problem 1:
Calculate the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray when a ray of light hits a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 40 degrees.
Problem 2:
Two rays of light strike a plane mirror. The first has an angle of incidence of 30 degrees and the second has an angle of incidence of 60 degrees. Calculate the angle between the two reflected rays.
Problem 3:
A candle is placed 25 cm in front of a plane mirror. A screen is placed 25 cm behind the mirror. Explain whether an image of the candle will be formed on the screen.
Problem 4:

Two plane mirrors are placed at right angles (90 degrees) to each other. A light ray strikes the first mirror at an angle of incidence of 30 degrees. Calculate the angle at which the light ray reflects from the second mirror. State the direction of the final reflected ray relative to the original incident ray.
Problem 5:
A person walks towards a plane mirror at a speed of 2 m/s. Calculate the speed at which their image appears to approach them.
Problem 6:

Describe the positions of the first three images formed in mirror A when two plane mirrors are placed parallel to each other, facing one another, with a small object placed between them 10 cm from mirror A and 30 cm from mirror B.
Problem 7:
Explain why you can read the word AMBULANCE written in reverse on the front of an ambulance when you see it in your car's rear-view mirror. Use the concept of lateral inversion in your answer.
Summary
Reflection occurs when a wave bounces off a surface at a boundary between two media.
The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (
\theta_i = \theta_r
), and the incident ray, reflected ray, and normal all lie in the same plane.
All angles are measured from the normal, not from the surface.
Regular (specular) reflection occurs on smooth surfaces and produces clear images.
Diffuse reflection occurs on rough surfaces and scatters light in many directions. It still obeys the law of reflection at each point.
A plane mirror produces a virtual, upright, laterally inverted image that is the same size as the object and the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.
Virtual images cannot be projected onto a screen because the light rays do not actually pass through the image location.
Ray diagrams use at least two rays from the object to locate the position and properties of the image.

\theta

A mirror only half a person's height is sufficient to see a full-length image.
